title: what the Rig Veda is
hook: a match struck in a dark kitchen. The Rig Veda's very first hymn begins with fire

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandukya Karika's last image: a firebrand whirled into circles, then held still, and a bow at the end. Did a circling worry slow down for even one breath? Day one thousand two hundred forty-four.
screen: `THE MANDUKYA KARIKA: THE TORCH HELD STILL.`

segments.voice: Before dawn, in a dark kitchen, someone strikes a match. There's the scratch, the little flare, the smell of it. They touch it to a lamp's wick, or to the burner under the morning's tea, and the room changes. Faces appear. The kettle appears. The day has started. Fire does that. It's often the first thing awake in a house. So it may not be a surprise where the Rig Veda begins. Not with a law, not with a list, not with the making of the world. Its first hymn opens with a single name: Agni. The fire. Today, a new part of the path: the Vedas themselves, and what the Rig Veda is.
screen: `A MATCH IN A DARK KITCHEN.` → `OFTEN THE FIRST THING AWAKE.` → `THE FIRST HYMN: AGNI.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. In the Sanskrit dictionaries, rig is a verse of praise, and veda is knowing. So the Rig Veda is knowledge carried in verses of praise. It's not a story told from start to end, and it's not a book of rules. It's a collection of hymns, made to be chanted aloud, addressed to many gods. And the collection opens with fire. In paraphrase, the first line says: I praise Agni, the household priest set in front, the god of the offering, the one who calls the gods, the richest giver of treasure. Notice the jobs piled onto that one flame. Agni is the fire on the altar. He's the priest at the ritual. He's the one who calls out to the other gods and carries the offering up to them. Fire is the go-between, the place where earth and heaven meet. The next verse says Agni is worthy of praise by the seers of old, and by new ones too. So the first hymn already sets its own singers beside the seers who came before. And then the hymn's last verse turns tender. Be easy to reach, it asks Agni, as a father is to his son. Stay with us, for our good. The book's first hymn ends by asking the fire to come close. Fire still has a place in Hindu rites today: a wedding fire, a lamp waved before a deity, an offering poured into a havan.
screen: `RIG: PRAISE. VEDA: KNOWING.` · `A COLLECTION OF HYMNS, CHANTED.` · `AGNI: FIRE, PRIEST, GO-BETWEEN.` · `EASY TO REACH, AS A FATHER IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a flame, or the thought of one. If it's safe and you have one, light a candle or a lamp. If not, call one to mind. Watch it. See how it moves without going anywhere, how it lights what's near it. Feel the warmth, real or remembered, on your face. Then let a person come to mind who is easy to reach, someone you can always call. Rest with the flame and that person together. If you pray, you can greet the fire in your own way. The bell holds the time.
What the Rig Veda is. Knowledge in verses of praise, a collection of hymns made to be chanted, opening with a hymn to Agni, the fire. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT THE RIG VEDA IS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what the Rig Veda is. Today, when you light a stove or switch on a lamp, remember that this collection of hymns begins with a flame, asked to stay close. Day one thousand two hundred forty-four.

screen: `DAY 1244 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT THE RIG VEDA IS.`

howItsDone: The Rig Veda's hymns are chanted rather than read silently, and fire remains central to Hindu ritual: a fire is kindled at weddings and in the havan, and lamps are waved before deities in worship.

original.note: Sanskrit: from rich, a verse of praise, and veda, knowing. The name of the collection of hymns.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Rig Veda is an ancient rulebook.
what it means: it's knowledge in verses of praise, a collection of chanted hymns, opening with fire.

notes: Rig Veda 1.1.1, 1.1.2 and 1.1.9 paraphrased (Griffith 1896 is public domain but not on the validator list; nothing quoted). Confirm 'richest giver of treasure' for ratnadhatama (the superlative is in the verse).
Name gloss (rc = verse of praise, veda = knowing) is attributed to the Sanskrit dictionaries (Monier-Williams 1899). Confirm the claims rule is satisfied by this citation, or cut the gloss.
'Fire is still near the center of Hindu rites today' (wedding fire, arati lamp, havan) is general description, not from the cited text. Confirm wording.
Original: Rigveda (ऋग्वेद); confirm Devanagari and pronunciation guide.

Editor: untangled the garbled name gloss ('a rich, spoken rig'); cut the overreach that 1.1.2 expects 'people not yet born' (the verse says seers old and new); softened 'near the center' of Hindu rites.
